transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Yeah, thanks. Well, I ended up calling the EAP at work because... lately, every little bang in the office just sets me off. Like, if someone shuts a file drawer too hard, or drops a coffee mug, I jump really hard. And then my chest just keeps racing for way longer than it should. It's just getting to be too much, so I figured I should come in.
Did this jumpiness and racing heart start after any particular stressful or frightening event happened to you, or has it built up gradually without one clear trigger?
It definitely started after something specific. This has been going on for about two weeks now, ever since I had this really intense late-night confrontation with my regional boss.
During that confrontation with your boss, did you feel like your life or physical safety was actually in danger at any point?

No, not really. I mean, he didn't threaten to hit me or anything like that. It was just... a really aggressive, loud argument, and we were the only ones left in the office at that point. But no, I never thought he was actually going to physically hurt me.
Since that confrontation, have you found yourself avoiding your boss, the office, or reminders of that night, or having unwanted memories or images of it popping into your mind?

No, I haven't really had that happen. I mean, I still go into the office every day, and I don't go out of my way to avoid him or anything. And I don't really get unwanted memories or pictures of the argument popping into my head, either. It's really just that jumping at loud noises that I mentioned.
Has this jumpiness and racing heart been affecting your ability to concentrate at work or interfering with your daily activities and relationships?

Yeah, it definitely is. I mean, I’m still making it to work every day, but... my concentration is just off. I'm noticeably slower with the accounts and when I have to make staffing decisions. I’ve actually had to ask my team to double-check things that I’d normally just handle on my own. And with performance reviews coming up, I’m really worried that these mistakes could end up affecting my job.
Since the confrontation, have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?

No, my sleep has been pretty normal, actually. I haven't had any trouble falling asleep, and I usually sleep through the night just fine. It's really just during the day when I'm awake that I feel so on edge.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient developed marked hyperarousal symptoms (exaggerated startle response, prolonged tachycardia to minor stimuli) within two weeks of an identifiable psychosocial stressor (an intense confrontation with his boss) that did not involve threat to life or physical safety, ruling out PTSD/ASD which require a criterion A traumatic event (actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence). The temporal link to a stressor within 3 months, marked distress/impairment out of proportion to the stressor, and duration of about 2 weeks (less than 6 months) fits best with Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) rather than a Generalized Anxiety Disorder (which would require broader, longstanding worry unrelated to a specific stressor) or PTSD.
